title: Maharashtra's Varkari
hook: a silver palanquin in a sea of white caps, and inside it, a pair of sandals

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maharashtra's Varkari and one tender word, mauli, passed from the god to the saint to the stranger on the road. Who did you greet like family? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

A palanquin is coming down the road, decorated and gleaming, carried on shoulders and pulled along in the middle of an enormous crowd. People press close just to touch it. Some bow as it passes. Some are crying. A child is lifted up to see. And inside, on a cushion, under flowers, is a pair of sandals. No king, no image, no person. Just sandals. To the crowd, that's not an empty seat at all. Today, the palkhi, and who is riding in it.
screen: `A PALANQUIN IN THE CROWD.` → `PEOPLE PRESS TO TOUCH IT.` → `INSIDE: A PAIR OF SANDALS.`

segments.voice: A palkhi is a palanquin, and on the wari the great palkhis carry the padukas, the sandals, of the saints. One sets out from Alandi with Jnaneshwar's padukas. Another sets out from Dehu, Tukaram's village, with his. Others come from the towns of other saints. The dindis you met earlier this week walk with them, in order, singing. Why sandals? In Hindu traditions, the feet of a teacher are honored, and sandals stand for the feet, for the one who walked in them. Bowing to a guru's sandals is a way of bowing to the guru. So when Varkaris carry Jnaneshwar's padukas toward Pandharpur, they're not carrying a souvenir. They're walking with Jnaneshwar. And tradition goes further. Varkaris speak of Jnaneshwar's samadhi at Alandi as a living one: tradition says he sat down in a chamber there, still alive, and was sealed in, and that he is still present. So when his palkhi leaves Alandi, the saint himself is going on pilgrimage, again, to the god he sang to. Now look at what that does to the walker. You're not only walking toward Vitthal. You're walking beside Jnaneshwar, or Tukaram, the way their first friends did. The saints aren't behind glass. They're on the road, in the middle of the crowd, carried on people's shoulders. And there's one more scene the palkhi brings. At open grounds along the way, the walkers form a great circle called a ringan, and a horse runs around it, a horse tradition links to the saint. People wait for the dust it kicks up and touch it to their foreheads. Even the dust is a blessing, because the saint passed by.
screen: `THE SAINTS' SANDALS IN A PALANQUIN` · `SANDALS STAND FOR THE FEET` · `JNANESHWAR STILL PRESENT` · `THE RINGAN AND ITS DUST`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your feet rest flat. Bring to mind a person who walked ahead of you and taught you something you still use: how to cook a dish, how to tie a knot, how to keep going. Picture their shoes, the ones they wore most. Think of the roads those shoes walked, and if thanks comes, let it. Then notice that some of what they knew is walking with you now, in your own habits. If you pray, you can give thanks for them in your own way. The bell holds the time.
Maharashtra's Varkari. The walkers who carry their saints' sandals in palanquins to Pandharpur, so the saints walk with them. Today's word.
Your line: Maharashtra's Varkari. Today, do one thing the way someone who taught you did it, and let them come along. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: On the wari, palanquins carrying the padukas of Jnaneshwar from Alandi and Tukaram from Dehu lead the singing dindis to Pandharpur, with ringan circles held along the way.

original.note: palkhi in Marathi, written in Devanagari: the palanquin that carries a saint's padukas on the wari.

trapdoor: what you thought: a palanquin carries a king or a bride.
what it means: on the wari, it carries a saint's sandals, and the crowd walks with the saint.
what a scholar hears: sandals standing for the teacher's feet, and a living samadhi that lets Jnaneshwar himself join the pilgrimage.

sources.ref: the palkhis of Jnaneshwar (Alandi) and Tukaram (Dehu); padukas; the ringan

notes: 'Others come from the towns of other saints': many palkhis join the wari (e.g. Eknath's from Paithan, Nivruttinath's from Trimbakeshwar); confirm whether to name them.
Jnaneshwar's sanjivan (living) samadhi at Alandi is told as tradition says; confirm phrasing.
The ringan horse: tradition associates it with the saint (the 'mauli's horse'); confirm wording and the custom of touching the dust to the forehead.
Hook mentions the palanquin being carried and pulled; in current practice the palkhi often rides on a decorated cart drawn by bullocks. Confirm the description.
